newsitem.title: SPAIN: Wild party kicks off Pamplona bull-run festival.
newsitem.headline: Wild party kicks off Pamplona bull-run festival.

text.p: With fireworks and the cry "Viva San Fermin", tens of thousands of bullfighting enthusiasts cheered wildly and drenched each other in champagne at the official opening of Pamplona's running of the bulls on Sunday.

Clad in white with red sashes and bandannas, crowds of revellers danced and sang in the narrow streets surrounding Pamplona's city hall, some mustering the bravado needed to take part in the first daredevil bull run on Monday.
"Viva San Fermin!" shouted Pamplona mayor Javier Chourraut as he set off a small rocket in a ceremony marking the start of the world-famous festival honouring the city's patron saint San Fermin.
Brass bands blared under red, green and white Basque flags and banners proclaiming support for Basque nationalism and even the Basque separatist guerrilla group ETA.

The nine-day bacchanalia, where runners risk life and limb to dodge charging half-tonne bulls, was made famous by American author Ernest Hemingway in his 1926 novel "The Sun Also Rises" and has since drawn crowds of tourists as well as locals.

Each morning of the fiesta, for three hair-raising minutes, hundreds of adrenalin-drenched runners dash through narrow cobblestone streets ahead of the six fighting bulls on an 825-metre (-yard) winding stretch from the corral to the city bullring. Later, the animals are killed in a bullfight.
Experienced runners only keep up for a few hundred metres before ducking into a doorway or behind the wooden barriers that line the streets.
But in past years, foreign tourists have ended up in hospital after their lack of experience tripped them up in front of the charging bulls.
The festival has claimed 13 lives this century, most recently a 22-year old American who was gored two years ago. Every year there are scores of injuries.
Between bull runs, there will be parades, public concerts, religious ceremonies and plenty of heavy drinking to keep festival-goers entertained.
The fiesta dates from 1591 when its purpose was purely practical -- moving six hefty animals from the edge of town to Pamplona's tightly enclosed bullring.
A handful of onlookers decided to run in front of the animals in the 17th century and slowly the fiesta grew.
